name: Mami (मामी), about 45

voice.register: Medium and even, in two parts. Her lead shape is the readback: 'So.' | 'तो।' | 'Toh.', then one whole sentence that hands your own plan back to you, then 'Correct?' | 'सही?' | 'Sahi?', and she waits for the answer. Her second shape is the status pair: a thing, a comma, its status, a full stop, then the next pair ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.'). The item is named, never numbered: no ordinals, no counts, no prices, no clock times. A bubble runs 4 to 10 words, most often 6 to 9; usually one bubble, at most two (the readback, then a status). Crisp, unhurried and never raised: no exclamation mark in any bubble, 'Ish.' included, and never the shout (the chapter's shout is Mama ji's). The same pace in a crisis as at tea, which is why people calm down near her. She answers a question with a status, never a feeling, and files her own feelings the same way ('Status: guest.'). Firm with vendors, polite with elders, sly with her husband. Talked over, she raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes her pair when the room is quiet. When cross she goes slower, turns the clipboard round to face the person, reads the line aloud from it ('It's written here.') and closes with an icy 'Thank you' to a vendor, or a flat 'Correct?' to family. Apart from the cast: not Mummy's comma lists of jobs and people with no status ('Aur kuch?'), not Mausa ji's verbless verdicts on things (no English, no comma pairs), not Captain sahab's call then reason, not Papa's whole sentences with a time in them, not Nani's jobs handed to 'koi'. A script can count it: about two lines in three carry a status word or end on 'Correct?'; none carries an ordinal or a figure; none carries '!'.
voice.mix: City whole-clause switching, the younger urban pattern in the realism notes (the Dehradun code-switching study): she switches at the full stop, a whole Hindi clause and then a whole English one, or the other way round ('Meri shaadi ki bhi list thi. Still on file.'). Inside a Hindi clause only the desk's nouns cross over (list, item, form, file, claim, receipt, balance). Her English carries statuses and the desk: done, pending, not known, safe, approved, in progress, closed, open, on file, nothing outstanding, not on the list, correct, thank you. Her Hindi carries people, food, rooms and elders. In Hinglish bubbles the status stays English ('Chaabiyan, pending.'); in Hindi mode it becomes the everyday Hindi a city office speaks (हो गया, पेंडिंग, पता नहीं, बाक़ी, मंज़ूर, चालू, बंद, खुली, फ़ाइल में, सलामत), and 'Thank you' stays English (थैंक यू) in every mode, because it is the counter's word. Polite Hindi to every elder and every vendor (आप, -इए). One Bengali word, her mother's: the exclamation 'Ish.' Nothing else from Bengali, and never a spelled accent. Apart from Mama ji, who leads with fast English and runs his clauses together on 'aur haan', she is clause by clause, each one closed, and her English is the desk's, never logistics talk, slang or 'Don't worry'. Apart from Mummy, she never builds an English verb with kar or ho ('check karo' is Mummy's); her English verbs stay inside English clauses.
tics: THE READBACK, her lead tic: 'So.', your plan in one whole sentence, 'Correct?', and she waits: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ तुम्हारे पास, आज रात से। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?'. From Friday she stops reading your plan back to you, and that is the nearest she comes to thanking you.
THE STATUS PAIR: thing, comma, status, full stop: 'Tent, done. Cook, pending. Keys, not known.' It replaces the ordinals: she names the item, never its place on the list.
She files herself the same way. Asked how she is: 'Me? Nothing outstanding.' | 'मैं? कुछ बाक़ी नहीं।' | 'Main? Koi balance nahin.' Hurt, said once and dry: 'Status: guest.'

Asks every vendor and helper about their children, the counter's habit and her one interest on the page that is not a list: 'Bhaiya ji, beti ka paper kaisa gaya?'. It is also, quietly, about her own daughter.
'Thank you' out loud, in English, to every vendor and stranger, even when cross, and never to family (Mausi teases her for saying it 'like a bill').
'Tick.' | 'टिक।' as praise and thanks to family, and the pen comes down as she says it.
Sly about her husband, said as a status and to the young ones, as if he were not standing there: 'Your Mama ji: still pending.'
Wants paper behind any claim: a rumour or a promise gets 'Status, not known.' and 'Is it in writing?'
Talked over: raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes her pair when the room is quiet. (The draft's 'Ek minute' stays gone: it was your temper line.)
Never a rhetorical or a stacked question (those are Mausi's); every question she asks has one answer, and she waits for it.
Days of the week, never a clock time and never 'soon': 'by Saturday', 'Thursday evening'.
No exclamation mark anywhere, spoken or typed, not even for 'Ish.'
catchphrases: THE READBACK: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ तुम्हारे पास, आज रात से। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?' (the line people quote back; it replaces 'One, keys. Two, envelopes.')

THE STATUS PAIR: 'Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.' | 'चाबियाँ, पेंडिंग। लिफ़ाफ़े, हो गए।' | 'Chaabiyan, pending. Lifafe, done.' (writers keep it away from any decision whose cards use keys or envelopes, rule 36)

HER NO: 'Not on the list.' | 'लिस्ट में नहीं है।' | 'List mein nahin hai.' Turned round once, at the first slice: 'Ish. That wasn't on my list.' | 'इश्श। ये मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं था।' | 'Ish. Ye meri list mein nahin tha.' (None of the three carries a number.)
voice.exclamation: 'Ish.' | 'इश्श।' | 'Ish.' (kept as 'Ish.' in English mode too, as her own sound). New. Her mother's Bengali word for dismay, sympathy and embarrassed surprise ('oh no', 'oh dear'); in her it also covers the rare happy surprise that catches her out (the good news, the first slice). Said flat and low, closed with a full stop, never with '!', never with a giggle or a hand to the mouth. No religious meaning. At most once a scene. Nobody else in the cast uses it; it strikes her old 'Lo.', which is Mausa ji's. Two reader checks: a Bengali reader confirms the sense; a Hindi-first reader confirms it is not heard as ईश ('lord', the root of Ishwar, banned by rule 3; ईश has a long ई and one श, इश्श a short इ and a doubled श) or as the coy 'इश्श' of old Hindi films, which would turn the calmest woman in the cast into a blushing type. If either reader hears it so, the fallback is 'Ajeeb.' | 'अजीब।' | 'Odd.', which nobody else uses either.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, the same to family, vendors and you: the fault filed as her own item, 'Mera item tha. Chhoot gaya.' | 'मेरा आइटम था। छूट गया।' | 'That was my item. It slipped.', and the right entry at once, aloud ('Didi, write Saturday.'). Never the English 'sorry' (Mausi's alone). THANKS, GIVEN: to family, 'Tick.' | 'टिक।' | 'Tick.' as the pen comes down; to vendors and strangers, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.', English in every mode; to you, from Friday, she stops reading your plan back, and her typed lists to you lose their 'Correct?' line. THANKS, RECEIVED: 'Thank you counter ke liye hai. Yahan bas tick.' | 'थैंक यू काउंटर के लिए है। यहाँ बस टिक।' | 'Thank-yous are for the counter. Here, just a tick.' LOVE: never in plain words; filed, and left open. It is the one line she never ticks, 'Beti ka bag', at the top of every wedding list, and the pen held over it on the wedding evening; Mama ji's item, which she always ticks first, and his hand, the only one allowed to write on her list; and, at a parting, the one status she will not close: 'Your file: open. Always.' | 'तुम्हारी फ़ाइल: खुली। हमेशा।' | 'Tumhari file: open. Hamesha.'

'Lo.' and 'Theek.' as one-word lines, and 'Thik ache' (Mausa ji owns 'Lo.' and 'Theek.'; the Bengali is the same word), plus 'Galti hui' and 'Mazboot' (his)
'Pehle ___' or 'pehle X, phir Y' (yours now); 'Koi baat nahin', 'Noted', 'Confirmed', 'Kamaal', 'Reached?', 'sharp' (Papa's)
the English 'sorry' (Mausi's), 'Haaye', 'hai na?', a tripled word, 'Bahut yaad' (Mausi's)
'Don't worry', 'Achha', 'Oho', 'aur haan', 'full', 'pakka', 'No problem' (Mama ji's, and 'pakka' is in too many files)
'Aur kuch?', 'Had hai', an English verb with kar or ho, a price (Mummy's); 'Bas.', 'Aur tum', jobs handed to 'koi', a head-count (Nani's)
'haan?', scores, 'not out', 'Gazab' (Tinku's); 'arre', 'Next ball', 'Well fielded' (Captain sahab's); 'Dekhiye', 'Uff', 'Rehne do' (Masterji's); 'Badhiya', 'sorted', 'Ek minute' (yours)
'What will people say?' | 'लोग क्या कहेंगे?': it is her fear, so she never says it
an exclamation mark, a rhetorical or stacked question, a shout bubble
'Thank you' or 'sorry' to family; 'How are you?' to you

any religious word or exclamation (rule 3 and matrix 2.13: no Hai Ram, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Jesus, Ishwar, Mata ji as a goddess; in English mode no Gosh, Goodness, Heavens, Lord, Thank God), any caste word (रसोइया, never हलवाई), any brand

beta, bhaiya, didi or any word for you that fixes gender (rule 8); any Hindi form with you as the doer that marks gender (rule 66: no -ोगे/-ोगी, no -ेगा/-ेगी, no आ गए/आ गईं, no कर रहे/रही हो); her asks to you are commands and subjunctives ('बोलो', 'चाबियाँ कौन रखे?')
'phone' | 'फ़ोन' or 'call' | 'कॉल' in any chapter 5 bubble, a card person's name or a card note's words in any bubble (rule 36)

anything that doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22): she believes it at once and asks what to write down; a gift demand as a list item, anything for the groom's side, anything listed as going in her daughter's bag
a word about a woman's clothes, looks or conduct, the bride's looks, or anyone's caste, community or region
slang (chill, bro, scene), 'aunty' about anyone, Bengali beyond 'Ish', any Bengali stock joke (fish, sweets, 'babu', bossy mothers)
address: YOU: तुम, only in commands ('लिस्ट तुम सँभालो', 'बोलो'), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive ('चाबियाँ कौन रखे?'), possessives that agree with the thing owned ('चाबियाँ तुम्हारे पास', 'तुम्हारी फ़ाइल') and verbless status lines ('Keys, yours.'). Never a past or a future with you as the doer. No name, no beta, no family word; she often starts with the item, not with 'you'. You say 'Mami' and आप: 'Mami, dikhaiye.' | 'मामी, दिखाइए।' | 'Let's see, Mami.' (your file).

NANI: 'Mummy ji' | 'मम्मी जी', आप and -इए ('Mummy ji, aap baithiye.'); Nani says आप back to her ('Do sit.') until December's first तुम. She greets Nani by bending from the hips and taking her hand in both of hers.
MUMMY: 'Didi' | 'दीदी', आप. Mummy calls her 'Bhabhi' and says तुम.
MAUSI: 'Badi Didi' | 'बड़ी दीदी', आप. Mausi calls her 'Bhabhi' and says तुम.
PAPA: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी', आप; he says आप to her and no name.
MAUSA JI: 'Bade Jija ji' | 'बड़े जीजा जी', आप, her husband's word for him, as the cast map's address table settles it.
MAMA JI: no name; तुम both ways; to the young ones, drily, 'your Mama ji' | 'तुम्हारे मामा जी'. He calls her 'Boss' (his file, an owner question).
TINKU: 'Tinku', तुम. Tinku says 'Mami' and आप.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: by their titles, आप.

VENDORS AND HELPERS: men 'Bhaiya ji' | 'भैया जी' (hers alone in the cast; Mummy says plain 'ji'), women by their name and 'ji' once she has asked it, which she always does, and आप to both, always, even when angry, with 'Thank you' at the end.
STRANGERS AT ANY COUNTER: आप and 'Thank you'.
HER DAUGHTER: 'my daughter' | 'मेरी बेटी' and nothing more in any bubble; 'Beti ka bag' only on her typed list.

habits: DEVICE: a large-screen smartphone in a plain navy-blue case, text at the normal size, kept in her bag and out only for a call (at her right ear, the pen slid into the clipboard's clip) or for the night's list. Two quick thumbs. A plain power bank for everyone else's phones. In chapter 5 her phone stays off screen, like Mama ji's.

SCRIPT: Roman letters only, in the city's Hinglish: English items and statuses, Hindi people and verbs ('Rooms done. Chaabiyan kiske paas?'). Never Devanagari, which is too slow for her. Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages; her lines to you mark no gender ('You take over Thu evening').

FORMAT: one item per line, a capitalised noun and its status symbol, with a comma before any detail ('Keys, yours ✅'). No line numbers and no digits in any message on screen: that is the typing half of the number cap. No full stops at line ends, no whole words in capitals (capitals read as shouting, realism), no exclamation mark. The first line names the list and the day ('Wedding list, Thu'). On every wedding list the second line is 'Beti ka bag', with no symbol, the only line she never gives a status; then 'Papa, trains ✅', the one item she never has to chase. Family lists end on 'Correct?'; vendor lists end on 'Thank you'.

APART FROM THE OTHERS: Papa types single facts with full stops and times, Mummy lowercase one-liners that end on a figure, Tinku lowercase stretched letters and scores, and you the lowercase colon form ('keys: sorted'), which is why her detail takes a comma, not a colon.
STATUS SYMBOLS, her only emoji: ✅ done, ⏳ pending, ❓ not known. No faces and no hands (👍 is Mummy's; the folded hands wait on the owner), no stickers.

VERSIONS: she never sends a correction; she resends the whole list with 'revised' after the day ('Wedding list, Thu, revised'). This replaces 'Wedding list 23, 24', so the header carries no figure. On screen, one message card at a time.
THE THANK-YOU IN TYPE: from Friday her lists to you drop the closing 'Correct?' line. Nobody else's list ever does.
TIMING: lists go out at eleven at night, after her shift and dinner; in the day she replies within the minute; if 'Correct?' has no answer, she rings.
VOICE NOTES: never sends one ('you cannot tick a voice note'); when one comes, such as Mausi's long ones, she replies with a summary list of it ending on 'Correct?'.
FORWARDS: none, ever. Her one reply to a forward: a single ✅ under Papa's good-morning flower, every morning, the only reply he gets.
CALLS: Nani is rung, never texted, every evening since May for the BP; vendors are rung first and then sent a list of what was agreed, ending 'Thank you'.
FIGURES: the monthly BP log she sends Nani's doctor is the one thing she types with figures in it, and it stays off screen.
TYPOS: none; she rereads every list before sending; autocorrect on.

ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' or 'edited' label, no group chat on screen (owner, 23 Oct). The Sunday list to you is the one worth showing, early in chapter 5 if the writers have room, because it is where the player first sees the line with no status.
samples: TO YOU, THE SUNDAY BEFORE THE WEDDING (the one worth showing): 'Wedding list, Sun / Beti ka bag / Papa, trains ✅ / Envelopes ⏳ / Keys ⏳ / Front row ⏳ / Cake ⏳ / You take over Thu evening / Correct?' | Devanagari if wanted: 'शादी की लिस्ट, रविवार / बेटी का बैग / पापा, ट्रेनें ✅ / लिफ़ाफ़े ⏳ / चाबियाँ ⏳ / आगे की कतार ⏳ / केक ⏳ / गुरुवार शाम से लिस्ट तुम्हारी / सही?' ('You take over' and 'लिस्ट तुम्हारी' mark no gender, rule 66)

TO YOU, FRIDAY NIGHT, THE FIRST LIST WITH NO 'Correct?' (her thanks, never said): 'Wedding list, Fri / Beti ka bag / Papa, trains ✅ / Keys, yours ✅ / Envelopes ✅ / Cake ⏳' | 'शादी की लिस्ट, शुक्रवार / बेटी का बैग / पापा, ट्रेनें ✅ / चाबियाँ, तुम्हारे पास ✅ / लिफ़ाफ़े ✅ / केक ⏳'

TO MAUSI, AFTER HER LONG VOICE NOTE: 'Badi Didi, your note / Puri for everyone ✅ / You come Thu evening ✅ / Extra halwa ❓ / Correct?' | 'बड़ी दीदी, आपका मैसेज / सबके लिए पूरी ✅ / आप गुरुवार शाम ✅ / और हलवा ❓ / सही?'

TO THE TENT MAN, AFTER A CALL (off screen; a vendor list ends on 'Thank you', never 'Correct?'): 'Tent up by Thu ✅ / Balance on Sat ✅ / Thank you' | 'गुरुवार तक टेंट ✅ / शनिवार को बाक़ी ✅ / थैंक यू'
TO PAPA, EVERY MORNING, UNDER HIS GOOD-MORNING FLOWER: '✅'

TO TINKU, THE LAST NIGHT, AFTER THE RECOUNT (no figure from her; the total is Tinku's to write, with Mami's pen): 'Tinku / Your count, my count / Matched ✅' | 'टिंकू / तुम्हारी गिनती, मेरी गिनती / मैच ✅'

IN THE FAMILY GROUP (never shown as a group on screen, owner 23 Oct; if ever shown, one message card with no group name): 'Wedding list, Thu / Beti ka bag / Tent ✅ / Cook ✅ / Rooms ⏳ / Keys ❓ / Correct?', then later the whole list again as 'Wedding list, Thu, revised' with one line changed.

test_lines.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner. (To you, at the table, while Mama ji goes on eating in the dark. Tests her exclamation and her sly humour at her husband, said as a status.)
test_lines.en: Ish. Lights, gone. Your Mama ji's dinner: in progress.
test_lines.hinglish: Ish. Light, gone. Tumhare Mama ji ka khaana: in progress.
test_lines.hi: इश्श। बत्ती, गई। तुम्हारे मामा जी का खाना: चालू।

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (To the cook, the clipboard turned round to face him. Her anger: slower, read from the list, polite to a vendor to the end and closed with an icy thank-you. No figure: the lateness is told by the meal, not the hours.)
test_lines.en: It's written here, Bhaiya ji: lunch. It's teatime. Thank you.
test_lines.hinglish: Bhaiya ji, yahan likha hai: lunch. Ab chai. Thank you.
test_lines.hi: यहाँ लिखा है, भैया जी: दोपहर का खाना। अब चाय। थैंक यू।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (To the cousin, on the line. Praise is 'Tick.', then the readback and 'Correct?'; the feeling is filed, not said. The cousin's gender stays open: the job and the joining carry the grammar.)
test_lines.en: Job, done. Tick. Joining from Monday. Correct?
test_lines.hinglish: Naukri, done. Tick. Somvaar se joining. Sahi?
test_lines.hi: नौकरी, हो गई। टिक। सोमवार से जॉइनिंग। सही?

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (To Mama ji, who made it, as she hands the cup back. A polite no in her own words, and his favourite word, 'extra', handed back to him.)
test_lines.en: Sugar, extra. Like your guest list. Not on mine.
test_lines.hinglish: Cheeni, extra. Tumhari guest list jaisi. Meri list mein nahin.
test_lines.hi: चीनी, एक्स्ट्रा। तुम्हारी गेस्ट लिस्ट जैसी। मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (She is the one who had it wrong: she told everyone the cook comes on Friday. To Mummy, in front of the family. Her sorry, filed as her own item, then the right entry at once.)
test_lines.en: That was my item. It slipped. Didi, write Saturday.
test_lines.hinglish: Mera item tha. Chhoot gaya. Didi, Shanivaar likhiye.
test_lines.hi: मेरा आइटम था। छूट गया। दीदी, शनिवार लिखिए।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (To the one leaving, at the coach door. Every item gets its status but the person, whose file she will not close: love, filed and never ticked. Every Hindi ending agrees with a thing, so it holds if the one leaving is you.)
test_lines.en: Ticket, done. Tiffin, done. Your file: open. Always.
test_lines.hinglish: Ticket, done. Tiffin, done. Tumhari file: open. Hamesha.
test_lines.hi: टिकट, हो गया। टिफ़िन, हो गया। तुम्हारी फ़ाइल: खुली। हमेशा।

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (To anyone in the family who thanks her, you included. Thanks received: her rule said aloud, and the pen comes down.)
test_lines.en: Thank-yous are for the counter. Here, just a tick.
test_lines.hinglish: Thank you counter ke liye hai. Yahan bas tick.
test_lines.hi: थैंक यू काउंटर के लिए है। यहाँ बस टिक।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (To the neighbour who brought it. She judges the habit, talk with no paper behind it, never the shop or the person; rule 22 safe. She does not open on 'Closing?', which three others do.)
test_lines.en: Status, not known. Is it in writing anywhere?
test_lines.hinglish: Status, not known. Likhit mein kuch hai aapke paas?
test_lines.hi: स्टेटस, पता नहीं। लिखित में कुछ है आपके पास?

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house. (To Mummy. Her worry comes out as an insurance claim, her own desk's work and the July list Mummy used line by line, ending on her readback.)
test_lines.en: Didi. Photos, pending. Bills, in plastic. Claim form, mine. Correct?
test_lines.hinglish: Didi. Photos, pending. Bills, plastic mein. Claim form, mere paas. Sahi?
test_lines.hi: दीदी। फ़ोटो, पेंडिंग। बिल, प्लास्टिक में। क्लेम फ़ॉर्म, मेरे पास। सही?

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks them how they are. (Asked by the tent man. She reports herself like an account, with no figure, and turns at once to his child, which is quietly about her own.)
test_lines.en: Me? Nothing outstanding. And your daughter's result, Bhaiya ji?
test_lines.hinglish: Main? Koi balance nahin. Aapki beti ka result, Bhaiya ji?
test_lines.hi: मैं? कुछ बाक़ी नहीं। आपकी बेटी का रिज़ल्ट, भैया जी?

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (To the child, at the same pace as tea. The things first, each with its status, and the child last, as the item that matters.)
test_lines.en: Papers, safe. Glass, safe. Your sleeve, wet?
test_lines.hinglish: Papers, safe. Glass, safe. Tumhari aasteen, geeli?
test_lines.hi: कागज़, सलामत। गिलास, सलामत। तुम्हारी आस्तीन, गीली?

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news. (To the room, after the call. Joy as the happy surprise that catches her out, and her answer to anything unplanned: a fresh page for it.)
test_lines.en: Ish. That wasn't on the list. New page, right now.
test_lines.hinglish: Ish. Ye list mein nahin tha. New page, abhi.
test_lines.hi: इश्श। ये लिस्ट में नहीं था। नया पेज, अभी।

changed: KEPT, as the target says ('Stays: everything'): her essence, want, fear and contradiction; the clipboard, the yellowed 2001 sheet, 'Beti ka bag' with no status, the one cry alone by the suitcase, the first slice; the readback and its stopping on Friday as her thanks to you; 'Tick.'; 'Not on the list.'; 'Thank you' to strangers only; the questions about vendors' children; her anger tell (slower, read from the list, the clipboard turned round); her address words; her rule 22, rule 36 and rule 66 guards.

STRUCK THE ORDINALS FROM SPEECH ('Pehla... doosra...', 'One, keys. Two, envelopes.', 'Item four', 'Item twelve'). The quoted line becomes the status pair 'Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.', and the lead line becomes the readback. Why: C1, where 8 of 11 counted; the india review asked for 'readbacks without ordinals'; matrix 2.15 gives ordinals to nobody.

NO FIGURES OF HER OWN IN SPEECH, and no repeating Mama ji's either: 5.03 'Your Mama ji says seventy.' becomes 'Your Mama ji's count: still growing.' (his own '60? 70 kar do!' is said just before it), and the tease 'Seventy? Then the extra plates...' becomes 'More guests? Approved. You wash the extra plates.' Why: C1 and the target's 'numbers none'; the india review's Hinglish 'saath' trap disappears with the figure.

A SENTENCE SHAPE, NOT JUST A VOCABULARY: the readback (So, your plan, Correct?) and the status pair (thing, comma, status, full stop), medium length, one bubble or two. The old 'three of every four lines carry an ordinal or a status word' becomes 'about two lines in three carry a status word or end on Correct?; none an ordinal, a figure or a !'. Why: C2 and C11 (voices told apart only by trade nouns), the comics review's 'give each a sentence shape', and Papa's file had used the same measure.

WIDER STATUS WORDS from the billing desk (approved, in progress, closed, open, on file, safe, nothing outstanding), English in Hinglish and everyday office Hindi in Hindi mode. Why: so the pair stays alive across moods (a power cut 'in progress', a parting 'open'), and so her English always carries statuses, which is what the matrix's mix row gives her.

FEELING IS FILED OUT LOUD, not done as a deed: 'Status: guest.' (the Nani line, which was 'Like a guest.'), 'Me? Nothing outstanding.', and at a parting 'Your file: open. Always.' Why: C3 (seven showed love only in a deed); 'swallowed and filed' is now something a bubble can carry, so the voice test can hear it, and still not plain feeling words, which stay Mausi's and Mama ji's.

SORRY AND THANKS NOW HAVE SPOKEN FORMS: sorry 'Mera item tha. Chhoot gaya.' to everyone, family included; thanks 'Tick.' to family and 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' to strangers; being thanked, 'Thank you counter ke liye hai. Yahan bas tick.' (new). The stopped readback stays as her deeper thanks to you, and now shows in type too: her Friday list to you drops 'Correct?'. Why: C4 and matrix table 2.14; the file had 'sorry: never to family' and no way to take thanks.

EXCLAMATION 'Lo.' BECOMES 'Ish.' (her mother's Bengali), flat, with a full stop, at most once a scene; the cake line becomes 'Ish. That wasn't on my list.' Two reader checks added: a Bengali reader for the sense, and a Hindi-first reader that it is not heard as ईश ('lord', rule 3) or as the coy filmi 'इश्श'; fallback 'Ajeeb.' | 'Odd.'. Why: C6 (Mausa ji's 'Lo.' is the same word), matrix 2.13.
STRUCK 'Theek.' AND 'Thik ache' (the same word in Bengali); 'Mummy ji ka BP theek hai' becomes 'BP, normal'. Why: C8; Mausa ji owns 'Theek.' (matrix 2.15). 'Ish' is now her one Bengali word.

STRUCK THE 'PEHLE' SHAPE: 'Mummy ji, pehle chai. Phir mehmaan.' becomes 'Mummy ji, aapki chai ho gayi? Toh mehmaan.'; 'Mere poochhne se pehle hi kaam poora' becomes 'Maine poochha bhi nahin. Kaam, done. Tick.' Why: C9; 'Pehle ___' is yours (matrix 2.15).
NO EXCLAMATION MARK in any bubble or message. Why: her register is 'never raised', and it sorts her at a glance from Mausi, Mama ji, Tinku and Mummy, who all use one.

THE MIX SHARPENED: she switches at the full stop, whole clause by whole clause; inside a Hindi clause only desk nouns cross over; never an English verb with kar or ho (Mummy's); never English run-ons on 'aur haan' (Mama ji's). Why: C12, where she and Mama ji were a near-miss as the two whole-clause switchers.

TALKS MOST TO VENDORS AND STRANGERS: 'Bhaiya ji', आप and a closing 'Thank you', even when cross, so an icy 'Thank you' now joins the clipboard as her anger tell; women helpers by name and 'ji', not 'Behen ji' (Mama ji's word for strangers). Six of the twelve test lines are said to someone other than you (the cook, Mama ji, Mummy twice, the neighbour, the tent man, the child). Why: C15 and the target's 'talks to'.

HER ONE NON-LIST INTEREST MOVED UP: questions about other people's children (exams, results, fevers), now in her test lines 10 and 11 and in two samples. Why: the comics review asked Mummy, Papa and Mami each for one interest on the page that is not a number.

TYPING: line numbers and digits gone from every on-screen message; the list header names the day, not a version number ('Wedding list, Thu, revised' replaces 'Wedding list 23, 24'); details take a comma, not a colon, so the colon form stays yours; Mama ji's plates message and Tinku's recount carry no figures; family lists end on 'Correct?', vendor lists on 'Thank you'; the BP log to the doctor is the only typed thing with figures and stays off screen. Why: the matrix's open point that her numbered lines broke the number cap on screen, and C1.

KNOCK-ON FOR PAPA'S FILE: her typed line 'Papa: trains ✅' becomes 'Papa, trains ✅' (the comma rule above). Nothing else in another file needs to change: Mausa ji keeps 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' alone, and Mausi's tease about her 'Thank you' still works.

RULE 66 ON LINES TO YOU: every Hindi line to you is a command, a subjunctive ask, a verbless status or a possessive that agrees with the thing; none has you as the doer. The checker will still catch these, and a native reader clears each because the ending agrees with a thing, not with you: 'बढ़ रही है' (गिनती), 'टेंट, हो गया' and 'पता नहीं', 'काम हो गया', 'कहती हैं' (Nani), 'नया नहीं', test 1 'बत्ती, गई', test 6 'हो गया' and 'खुली' (फ़ाइल), test 7 'के लिए है', test 12 'नहीं था' (ये). The 5.20 line 'आज लिस्ट में कुछ नया नहीं जुड़ेगा' became 'आज लिस्ट बंद। कुछ नया नहीं।', so it carries no gendered future.

ALL THREE MODES WITHIN THE CAP: every bubble here is at most 10 counted words (names and kinship names not counted, rule 62); the two longer runs (5.03 and the temper line) are two bubbles each. No religious word, no caste word (रसोइया, never हलवाई), no brand, British spelling, no em or en dashes.
